title: Biosphere to Ecosystems

standard_text: The biosphere, biomes and ecosystems; abiotic factors (light, temperature, water, soil) and biotic factors; energy flow through food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids; nutrient cycles (carbon, water, nitrogen); South African biomes. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 10, Life Sciences: Biosphere to ecosystems)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): biomes, abiotic and biotic factors, food chains and webs, energy flow, pyramids and nutrient cycles. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Energy flows through an ecosystem; nutrients are recycled.
key_sub: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with abiotic factors such as light, water, temperature and soil. South Africa's biomes include the fynbos, savanna, grassland, Karoo, forest and desert.

Producers make food by photosynthesis; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. At each trophic level energy is lost as heat in respiration, so food chains are short. Carbon, water and nitrogen are recycled.

Example

Which organisms return nutrients to the soil?

Bacteria and fungi

Answer: decomposers

Example

Producers have 10 000 kJ. About how much reaches the herbivores?

About 10%

Answer: 1 000 kJ

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled like nutrients.
  • Drawing arrows from the eater to the eaten.
  • Thinking decomposers are not part of the food web.

faq.q: Why is the fynbos biome special?
faq.a: It is the Cape Floral Kingdom, with thousands of plant species found nowhere else on Earth.

faq.q: Why are there few top predators in an ecosystem?
faq.a: Little energy reaches the top of the food chain.

items.q: A population of 200 deer has 70 births, 25 immigrants, 20 deaths and 24 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 251.

items.q: Two species of honeyeater feed on the same flowers. What is this?
items.e: Competition between different species.

items.q: What is the carrying capacity of an environment?
c: the largest population it can support for a long time
the number of species it contains
the fastest rate at which a population can grow
items.e: Limited by food, water, space and other resources.

items.q: Which factor is density-independent?
c: predation that increases with prey numbers
disease spreading through a crowded colony
items.e: Drought affects a population whatever its density.

items.q: A tick feeds on the blood of a bandicoot. What is this relationship?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: Loggers clear a forest, and shrubs grow back. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: What is primary succession?
c: colonisation of bare rock or new land where there was no soil
regrowth of a forest after a bushfire
the arrival of predators in a new area
items.e: Lichens and mosses are pioneer species.

items.q: What is an ecological niche?
c: the food chain a species belongs to
the number of individuals of a species
the role of a species, including what it eats, where it lives and how it interacts with others
the place where a species lives only
items.e: The habitat is only part of the niche.

items.q: Male zebras fight for mates. What is this?
items.e: Competition within one species.

items.q: Wild dogs control zebra and fox numbers in some areas. What role does this suggest wild dogs play?
items.e: Apex predators shape the whole food web.

items.q: A predator–prey graph shows the predator population peaking after the prey population. Why?
c: the two populations are not linked
predators increase only after there is plenty of prey, then fall when prey run short
items.e: The cycles are linked but out of step.

items.q: Which interaction is shown when a lyrebird and a bandicoot both dig in the leaf litter for the same insects?
items.e: Two species use the same limited resource.

items.q: A new volcanic island rises from the sea. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which factor is density-dependent?
items.e: Its effect grows as the population becomes denser.

items.q: Reef-building corals and the algae (zooxanthellae) in their tissues both benefit. What is this relationship?
items.e: The algae give sugars; the coral gives shelter and nutrients.

items.q: What does the competitive exclusion principle state?
c: two species cannot share exactly the same niche for long in one place
items.e: One species will outcompete the other.

items.q: Lava cools into new bare rock. Lichens grow first. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Clownfish shelter in sea anemones and keep them clean; the anemone's stinging cells protect the fish. What is this relationship?
items.e: Both species benefit.

items.q: What is a keystone species?
c: a species found only in one place
a species whose effect on its ecosystem is much larger than its numbers suggest
the largest species in a food web
the most common species in an ecosystem
items.e: Removing it changes the whole community.

items.q: A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps of its food; the shark is not affected. What is this relationship?
items.e: One benefits, the other is unaffected.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 50 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the tuna?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Chloe's energy pyramid shows 1 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 1 000 → 100.

items.q: The grass capture 5 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snakes?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: The algae capture 2 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snails?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: Lindiwe's energy pyramid shows 5 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 5 000 → 500 → 50.

items.q: Kgomotso's energy pyramid shows 2 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2 000 → 200 → 20 → 2.

items.q: Daniel's energy pyramid shows 2 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2 000 → 200.

items.q: The algae capture 1 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snails?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 20 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the tuna?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Why are there few snakes compared with grass?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: Jabu's energy pyramid shows 2 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2 000 → 200 → 20.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 20 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the zooplankton?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: The oak leaves capture 20 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the songbirds?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: Why are there few foxes compared with oak leaves?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: What percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level?
The grass capture 1 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snakes?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Aisha's energy pyramid shows 1 000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 1 000 → 100 → 10.

items.q: The algae capture 50 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the crayfish?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: Where does most of the energy at each level go?
c: It stays stored forever in the top level.
It is lost as heat from respiration and in waste.
It is recycled back to the producers.
items.e: About 90% is used or lost each step.

items.q: The grass capture 20 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snakes?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 600 000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 600 000 × 0,12 = 6 000 J.

items.q: In a food web, what happens to the number of crickets if most of the frogs that eat them are removed?
items.e: Less predation lets the prey population grow.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 5 000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 5 000 × 0,12 = 50,0 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 10 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 10 × 10³ = 10 000 J.

items.q: What is a trophic level?
c: a feeding position in a food chain
the number of organisms in a habitat
items.e: Producers are level 1, herbivores level 2.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 60 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 60 × 10³ = 60 000 J.

items.q: What is the role of producers?
c: releasing all their energy as heat
converting light energy into chemical energy in organic molecules
items.e: Producers fix energy by photosynthesis.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 80 000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 80 000 × 0,12 = 800 J.

items.q: A single eucalyptus supports thousands of caterpillars. What shape is the pyramid of numbers?
c: inverted at the base (one producer, many consumers)
items.e: Pyramids of numbers can be inverted; pyramids of energy cannot.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 50 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 50 × 10³ = 50 000 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 70 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 70 × 10³ = 70 000 J.

items.q: The secondary consumers contain 20 000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the tertiary consumers contain 2 400 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 12,0%.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 90 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 90 × 10³ = 90 000 J.

items.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five links?
c: there is too much biomass at the top
plants cannot support more than one consumer
too little energy is left at the top to support another level
items.e: Energy decreases at each trophic level.

items.q: Which statement about matter and energy in ecosystems is correct?
c: matter is recycled, but energy flows through and is lost as heat
energy is recycled, but matter is lost
items.e: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 80 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 80 × 10³ = 80 000 J.

items.q: Which process returns nutrients from dead organisms to the soil?
items.e: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

items.q: The primary consumers contain 20 000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers contain 1 600 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8,00%.

items.q: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
c: all the energy is stored as biomass
much is used in respiration and released as heat, and some is in undigested waste
energy is destroyed at each level
items.e: Typically only about 10% passes to the next level.

items.q: Which pyramid can never be inverted?
items.e: Energy always decreases up the levels.

items.q: Where does burning fossil fuels move carbon?
c: from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into living things
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere.

items.q: Chloe observes: “Bacteria in soil change nitrogen into a form plants can use.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A dead tree's carbon is released by fungi. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Where does ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> move carbon?
c: from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
items.e: Ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> moves carbon from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil?
items.e: Decomposition.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from producers into consumers?
items.e: Animals eating plants.

items.q: What happens to the carbon in a dead tree?
c: It stays in the log forever.
Decomposers release it as CO<sub>2</sub>, which plants can use again.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Chloe observes: “A leaf falls and decomposers break it down.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Musa observes: “A fox breathes out carbon dioxide.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere?
c: formation of fossil fuels over millions of years
items.e: Volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Where does animals eating plants move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into living things
from dead organisms into the geosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
items.e: Animals eating plants moves carbon from producers into consumers.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the hydrosphere into the geosphere?
items.e: Shell-building sea animals forming limestone.

items.q: In a swamp with little oxygen, how do some bacteria break down matter?
c: anaerobic respiration, which can release methane
they cannot break it down at all
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Plankton remains are buried and pressed for millions of years. What forms?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Is energy recycled in an ecosystem?
c: No. Energy flows through and leaves as heat; matter is recycled.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Bongani observes: “A rabbit eats grass.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Where does forest fires move carbon?
c: from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from living things into the atmosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Forest fires moves carbon from living things into the atmosphere.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon in coal returns to the air at a power station. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Where does formation of fossil fuels over millions of years move carbon?
c: from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from dead organisms into the geosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
items.e: Formation of fossil fuels over millions of years moves carbon from dead organisms into the geosphere.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A carbon atom in CO<sub>2</sub> enters a grass leaf. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 900 000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 900 000 × 0,13 = 900 J.

items.q: What is the shape of the pyramid of energy?
items.e: The pyramid of energy: always upright.

items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 2 000 × 0,13 = 2,00 J.

items.e: The pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem: spindle-shaped (inverted in part).
